sentences.text: Tastavinsaurus was a medium-sized herbivorous sauropod dinosaur.
Scientists estimate this animal reached a length of 16 meters and weighed approximately 8 tonnes.
Its hind legs were built for stability rather than speed, featuring a tibia that measured only 55% of the femur's length.
The pubis bone was straight and ended in a distinctive long, upward-curving pointed tip.
A unique anterior chevron found between the third and fourth vertebrae had a Y-shaped profile ending in a plow-shaped blade.
The preserved portion of the tail extends for more than three meters.
This species represents the best-preserved Early Cretaceous sauropod skeleton known in Europe.
The genus name refers to the Tastavins river, where the word Tastavin means 'wine taster' in Catalan.
The remains consist of a partial skeleton discovered in the Early Cretaceous Xert Formation of Spain.
The holotype fossil, cataloged as MPZ-99/9, was found within a limestone layer dating to the Early Aptian.
This single individual includes essentially the posterior half of the skeleton, which spans ten meters in length.
Due to its completeness, it stands as one of the most complete sauropod skeletons known from Europe.
The type species Tastavinsaurus sanzi was formally named and described in 2008 by José Ignacio Canudo Sanagustín, Rafael Royo-Torres, and Gloria Cuenca-Bescós.
The specific name honors the Rio Tastavins in Spain and the paleontologist José Luis Sanz.
Initial reports of this discovery appeared in scientific literature in 1999.
The dorsal vertebrae are opisthocoelous and relatively short, a condition often associated with flexible necks in sauropods.
In the anterior tail region, the vertebrae are procoelous with flattened centra.
The spinous processes are positioned forward on the vertebral arch and are low and mace-shaped at the tail base, representing a basic trait of Macronaria.
Tastavinsaurus is classified as a sauropod dinosaur belonging to the clade Titanosauriformes.
Phylogenetic analysis identifies it as the sister taxon of the North American Venenosaurus within Titanosauriformes.
A 2011 analysis found Tastavinsaurus to be the sister species of Janenschia.
While originally described as a somphospondylan, recent studies suggest it may actually be a member of the Brachiosauridae family.
This dinosaur lived during the mid-Cretaceous, approximately 120 million years ago in the Aptian stage, in what is now Europe.
More precise dating places its existence between 121.4 and 119.57 million years ago during the Aptian stage.
It is currently debated whether Tastavinsaurus belongs to the Somphospondyli or the Brachiosauridae.
